Lay a document's contents out as printed pages

Source: R/layout.R
rtf_layout.Rd

Shows how the contents added by rtf_tables() and rtf_figures() fall on the pages generate_rtfreport() writes. Each content is a block; a block begins a page unless it was added with page_break = FALSE, in which case it goes on the page before it, under what is there. A table's own later pages (a plan's, or as_rtftables()'s) always begin a page, and so does the document's first content.

Usage

rtf_layout(doc)

# S3 method for class 'rtf_pages'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

doc

An rtf_document().

x

An rtf_pages object.

...

Unused.

Value

An rtf_pages object: a list with

pages

one entry per printed page, each a list with number (the page number, as rtf_section()(page = ) counts it), section (the section the page is in, counted from 1), section_start (TRUE where a section begins: page 1, a page rtf_section() starts one on, or a page an auto_section heading opens), section_label (that heading, or NULL) and segments: the blocks on the page, top to bottom, each a list with block (its position in the document), name, content (an rtftable or rtfplot), title (with cont_title's line on a table's later pages), footnote, space_before, group and page_in_group (which table, and which page of it), section (the auto_section heading the block opens, or NULL) and values (the columns its table was cut on and this page's value of each, a named character vector, or NULL: see Page values in rtf_tables()); and the page's own values: each column that of the first block on the page with a value for it.

n_blocks

the number of blocks.

paper

the page size and font size, for printing.

print() shows one line per block.

Details

A page has one auto_section heading (see rtf_tables()): that of the first block on it that has one. A later block on the same page with a different heading gets a warning, and its heading is not used; no page break is added for it. A page whose blocks have none stays in the section before it. An rtf_section()(page = n) on the page wins over its heading.

Nothing is measured: the pages are decided by page_break and by the tables' own pagination (max_rows, split, first_rows) alone. A page holding more than fits is carried on by the reader (Word, LibreOffice), and the page numbers written into the file are then off by those pages. Fitting a page is the program's to arrange; print() of the result shows the rows of each table and the size of each figure to arrange it by.

See also

rtf_tables() / rtf_figures() (page_break, space_before, first_rows), generate_rtfreport().

Examples

df <- function(n) data.frame(Item = sprintf("Row %02d", seq_len(n)), N = seq_len(n))
doc <- rtf_document() |>
  rtf_tables(list(Summary = df(8)), titles = "Table 1") |>
  rtf_tables(list(Listing = df(12)), titles = "Listing 1", page_break = FALSE) |>
  rtf_tables(list(Other = df(5)), titles = "Table 2")
lay <- rtf_layout(doc)
length(lay$pages)      # 2: the listing goes on the first page
#> [1] 2
lay
#> rtf_pages: 3 blocks on 2 pages (letter landscape, 9 pt)
#>  page 1  [sec 1]  Summary  rtftable 8 rows   title 1
#>       +           Listing  rtftable 12 rows  title 1
#>  page 2           Other    rtftable 5 rows   title 1
